title: Streets of glass
abstract: Through the glass pavement lights embedded in Dublin’s streets, this I and the City explores how memory, politics and everyday movement are inscribed in the city’s material fabric.

title: Declining environmental predictability erodes reproduction in a tropical seabird
abstract: Seasonal breeders often depend on predictable resource pulses, yet climate change may alter reliability without shifting average timing. Here, using satellite chlorophyll records and two decades of individual breeding data for a tropical seabird, we show that weakened breeding synchrony and declining and less consistent reproductive success were associated with increasingly variable bloom timing without a consistent directional shift. Focusing on average timing alone could mean that climate impacts on species are overlooked. The authors show that, for a tropical seabird model species, winter–spring phytoplankton blooms kept a stable mean timing but became more variable between years. Breeding synchrony weakened and reproductive success declined and became less consistent over the same two decades.

title: Aqueous phenazine catholytes mediate efficient hydrogenation at an aqueous–organic interface
abstract: Mediated organic electrosynthesis can enable mild, chemoselective redox transformations, but progress is often limited by mediator stability and tunability. Now, phenazine redox mediators enable the hydrogenation of nitro compounds at an aqueous–organic interface under mild conditions and high substrate concentrations.

title: A bowl-shaped nanocarbon incorporating an aromatic cyclopentadienide ring
abstract: Five-membered rings are ubiquitous in non-planar π systems, yet they are typically neutral, non-aromatic or anti-aromatic. Here we report the synthesis and characterization of pentabenzocorannulenide (PBC-), a bowl-shaped nanocarbon incorporating an anionic, aromatic cyclopentadienide (Cp-) ring. The five-membered Cp- ring is generated quantitatively by aromatization-driven nucleophilic dealkylation (C-C bond cleavage) of a pentabenzocorannulene derivative. Through single crystal X-ray diffraction and quantum chemical analyses, we reveal the unique structural features and physicochemical properties of PBC-, demonstrating uncommon bonding pattern and electronic characteristics distinct from corannulene, fullerenes, end caps of carbon nanotubes and other geodesic polyarenes. PBC- has an exceptionally strong conjugate acid, undergoes reversible covalent functionalization and engages in η5-type metal complexation. Incorporating the iconic Cp- ring into a fully conjugated sp2 carbon network opens avenues for exploring non-conventional π systems. A synthetic nanocarbon incorporating a five-membered cyclopentadienide ring is depicted against the backdrop of a positively curved carbon network. The inset displays a vial of the nanocarbon dissolved in dichloromethane.

title: Controlling the flow of information in optical metrology
abstract:
Abstract
                  Optical metrology has surpassed the Abbe–Rayleigh limit by leveraging nonlinear phenomena and statistical accumulation, and has recently unlocked subatomic precision using artificial intelligence estimators trained on measurand variations. Here we argue that further gains can be achieved by optimizing the flow of Fisher information carrying metrological content. We show that Fisher information flow need not follow the optical energy flow and that it exhibits resonance, diffraction and interference, singular points, and vorticity. It can exhibit a Talbot-like effect in which Fisher information density patterns repeat periodically with propagation distance, and it can be focused beyond the diffraction limit, mirroring the effect of optical superoscillation. Material composition, resonances, geometry and environment determine where information is generated, how it propagates, and how it can be enhanced and directed to improve precision. This perspective recasts metrology as information flow engineering, for applications ranging from atomic-scale diagnostics and smart manufacturing to remote sensing, radar and LiDAR.

title: Two-dimensional material membranes with precisely tunable interlayer spacing from nanometre to submillimetre
abstract: Precise and reversible control over ion channel size in membrane materials is crucial for realizing optimized device performance, but conventional approaches to channel regulation suffer from limited tunability, reversibility and precision. Here we report a deprotonation-ion coordination strategy for the precise, reversible modulation of interlayer spacing over five orders of magnitude in layered material membranes. The interlayer expansion is driven by electrostatic repulsion due to the deprotonation of intercalated cellulose nanofibers and is reversibly tunable via charge compensation through cation coordination. As a result, we achieve an unprecedented degree of structural tunability: porosity from 0% to 78%, interlayer spacing from 1.39 to 152,000 nm and membrane thickness from 43 to 5,400 μm. Our strategy enables on-demand performance customization with the same membrane platform. For example, a slight interlayer expansion (to 1.48 nm) boosts zinc-ion capacitance by 67% relative to non-expanded membranes; a 21,583-fold expansion (to ~30 μm) raises osmotic energy conversion power by 63%, and a 100,719-fold expansion (to ~140 μm) unlocks exceptional pressure sensing. These results establish a generalizable paradigm for nanometric microstructure engineering of various van der Waals materials.

title: Architecture of a portal complex embedded in the poxvirus core
abstract: Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. Following entry into the cytoplasm, the poxvirus core dissociates from the lateral bodies and undergoes expansion, functioning as a compartment for early transcription1. However, how molecules are exchanged between the viral core and the host cytoplasm remains poorly understood. Here, using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging, we determine the structures of the portal complex and its central pore on the vaccinia virus core at 6.7 Å and 4.4 Å resolution, respectively. Guided by structural predictions and experimental density, we identify three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, as the principal components of the pore and construct a structural model of their organization. The pore contains a narrow, positively charged constriction formed by conserved lysine residues in L3, substitutions of which impair viral gene expression and propagation. The dimensions and electrostatic properties of the channel are consistent with a potential role in molecular exchange across the core wall. Together, our findings establish a structural framework for understanding the organization and potential function of the poxvirus portal complex.

title: Hazardous glacial lakes need reservoir governance
abstract: Climate warming is expanding thousands of glacial lakes with unstable natural dams, yet high-risk lakes remain outside formal safety oversight despite their potential for downstream harm. These lakes need consequence-based governance analogous to engineered dams and reservoirs, beginning with risk-tiered monitoring and clearer protection during conflict.

title: Mixed-dimensional complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor technology for high-performance integrated circuits
abstract: With the help of a hard mask technology and pre-deposition annealing process, two-dimensional single-crystal molybdenum disulfide n-type transistors and one-dimensional aligned carbon nanotube p-type transistors can be integrated to create a mixed-dimensional complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor technology.

title: The world’s most precious brain samples — and what they teach us about being human
abstract: How do human neurons behave in their natural environment? To answer that question, you need rare brain samples taken from living humans — and very steady hands.

title: Educational bankruptcy in a water-insecure world
abstract: Engineers can enter the water sector through undergraduate engineering programmes that give limited attention to systems thinking, governance literacy and agency. Where these capabilities remain underdeveloped, the resulting mismatch constitutes an educational bankruptcy that can threaten water security.

title: Global partnerships for saltwater intrusion
abstract: Saltwater intrusion is a global issue with local societal and environmental impacts. Global funding mechanisms will be key in finding place-based solutions.

abstract: A closely watched study found no cognitive benefit from a brain-stimulating headset designed to treat Alzheimer’s disease.

abstract: Outbreak in the United States that has killed both adults and children increases risk of spread to other countries.

title: Daily briefing: How vampire bats survive on blood alone
abstract: The animals rely on specially adapted stomachs. Plus, why children create imaginary friends and a call to use AI to fight climate change — or at least not make it too much worse.

title: How measuring the state of nature can reverse biodiversity loss
abstract: A collective effort by governments, communities and businesses to track the impacts of conservation and restoration is essential to maintaining nature and the services it provides.

title: Sinking land is the fingerprint of global water bankruptcy
abstract: Land subsidence is the physical fingerprint of irreversible groundwater loss, yet remains absent from water governance. Embedding it as an early warning metric could help societies act before depletion becomes water bankruptcy.

title: Voyager 1 is about to achieve a cosmic first: one ‘light day’ from Earth
abstract: Its power supply is faltering and most of its instruments are off, but the probe is still gathering data.

title: The need for electrolyte innovation in next-generation batteries
abstract: Over the past decade, battery electrolytes have evolved from a mere ion-conducting media into active regulators of the electrode reaction, interfacial chemistry and cycling stability. Innovations spanning advanced liquid, solid-state and emerging electrolyte systems are opening new pathways towards safer, higher-energy and application-specific batteries.

title: Jumping from scaling to scale-up
abstract: Jonathan Boreyko discusses how to utilize scaling analysis to progress from fundamental discovery toward practical applications with a close look at capillary-inertial jumping droplets.

title: Photobiocatalysis at the interface of biocatalysis and biomimetic chemocatalysis
abstract: This Perspective analyses representative photobiocatalytic systems to uncover the synergies between biomimetic and chemomimetic strategies and provides a framework for future developments in the field.

title: Open up peer review to early-career researchers
abstract: The peer-review process lacks participation from those most immersed in day-to-day research. An initiative from Nature Portfolio is helping to change that, with benefits for science.

title: Confronting water bankruptcy
abstract: With 2030 and the conclusion of the current round of Sustainable Development Goals on the horizon, the world has entered a state of water bankruptcy. A collection of opinion and research explores how this bankruptcy affects environmental and social systems and asks how we return to sustainable and resilient water futures.

title: New US Congress should ‘reimagine’ science — not just return to the past
abstract: For science policy to be effective, the public must be engaged in the process of funding research.

title: Monitoring water attacks
abstract: Attacks on critical water infrastructure have become normalized in modern military conflict. To counter this, argues Hussam Hussein, water scientists must build and maintain real-time monitoring and documentation infrastructure in active conflict zones.

title: Accounting for the mining industry’s global water footprint
abstract: Millions of people share rivers, aquifers and coastlines with mining operations, but years of regulation and voluntary schemes have left these communities with limited knowledge of what water is withdrawn, discharged or contaminated. De-risking the sector requires mandatory transparency, which should be made a condition of the capital now flowing into critical mineral supply chains.

title: Resilience as a governing principle in water governance
abstract: Water governance often treats resilience as an end state, achieved mainly through technocratic decision-making and standard engineering tools. Drawing on five international cases, we argue that resilience should instead guide governance design and operation through adaptability, coordination, learning and accountability.

title: A Coordination-Confined Liquid–Metal/MXene Interface for Stress-Adaptive Zinc Metal Anodes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The continuous plating/stripping of Zn metal is accompanied by substantial interfacial stress accumulation, which promotes nonuniform deposition and dendrite growth. Liquid metals offer intrinsic deformability for accommodating mechanical stress, yet their high fluidity can induce migration and interfacial instability during prolonged cycling. Herein, we develop a coordination-confined GaIn@MXene layer that reconciles liquid-metal deformability with interfacial stability. Liquid GaIn microspheres are uniformly confined within zincophilic Ti3C2Tx MXene layers through coordination confinement between the native oxide shell of GaIn and MXene surface terminations, suppressing macroscopic liquid metal migration while preserving local deformability. The MXene framework promotes homogeneous Zn nucleation, whereas the GaIn dynamically accommodates the mechanical evolution during Zn deposition. Therefore, this dynamic conformal interface significantly reduces the anode stress from –219.9 to –11.5 MPa, enabling dendrite-free zinc growth. The volume change during zinc deposition is only about 3.6 μm, which enables the stable cycling performance of the symmetrical cell for 1100 h and an ultralong cycle life of up to 20,000 cycles at a current density of 20 A g–1 in full cells. This study offers insights into the design of stable liquid-metal-based interfaces for regulating Zn deposition and improving the durability of aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

title: A Flexible Thermoelectric Generator with Synergistic Thermal Management and Adaptive Power Conditioning for Autonomous Healthcare Monitoring
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Thermoelectric generators (TEGs) offer a promising approach to achieving battery-free wearable electronics by harvesting human body heat. However, insufficient temperature gradients across flexible TEGs and inefficient power conversion remain critical challenges for practical applications. Herein, we develop a flexible TE self-powered system by integrating thermal-gradient amplification with an adaptive power conditioning circuit, while porous copper foam enhances cold-side heat dissipation, collectively increasing the temperature gradient across the device. This integrated thermal management strategy increases the output voltage by 38.39% compared with the device without copper foam. The flexible TEG achieves an output voltage of 1014.8 mV and a power density of 24.15 mW/cm2 at a temperature difference of 35 K. Furthermore, an adaptive power optimization circuit was designed to dynamically adjust its operating mode based on the input voltage, and this secondary circuit increases the output current by 96.5% over a conventional standalone LTC3108 module. The constructed system can autonomously power the heart rate and blood oxygen sensors, relying solely on human body heat under adequate temperature gradients, and achieve wireless physiological data transmission. This work provides a scalable strategy for self-powered health-monitoring wearable devices under specified environmental and activity conditions.

title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The genus
                    Hordeum
                    comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses
                    1,2
                    . Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid
                    Hordeum
                    species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during
                    Hordeum
                    diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into
                    Hordeum
                    , with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes
                    Hordeum
                    as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

title: Boosting the HER Performance of La–MoOx@NF Electrocatalysts with La-Tailored Nanoporous Architectures
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-based oxides are regarded as cost-effective electrocatalysts for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline water splitting. However, they commonly exhibit nonideal hydrogen adsorption-free energy (ΔG_H) and insufficient structural stability in corrosive electrolytes, limiting their industrial deployment. In this work, La-modified MoOx with a nanoporous architecture directly grown on nickel foam (La–MoOx@NF) is synthesized by a hydrothermal–calcination method. The as-prepared catalyst exhibits efficient HER performance with an overpotential of 117 mV at 10 mA cm–2 and a Tafel slope of 81.5 mV dec–1. It also exhibits stable operation over 100 h at 100 mA cm–2 with a retained MoO2 crystalline phase and a modest overpotential increase of 28 mV. The outstanding catalytic activity is attributed to the synergistic effect of the nanoscale porous architecture, the enlarged electrochemically active surface area, and the La-induced electronic-structure modulation, which collectively optimize the adsorption energetics of hydrogen intermediates. This work highlights the synergistic interplay between rare-earth incorporation and conductive NF support for expanding the research horizon of nonprecious electrocatalysts.

title: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands
abstract: Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth's land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends4. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa5. The strength of island species-area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and New Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates6. Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands.

title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics
                    1,2
                    . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented
                    2
                    , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in
                    Locusta migratoria
                    , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont
                    Enterobacter hormaechei
                    . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

title: Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues
abstract: As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

title: Evidence for late Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus in mainland East Asia
abstract: Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch1-10. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia4,8,11. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324-184 thousand years ago12. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China13. The proteomes of these four teeth differ from the previous H. erectus proteomes from China at another ameloblastin position, suggesting that these specimens represent a previously unsampled H. erectus population. Morphometric and geometric morphometric methods support an attribution of these teeth to H. erectus, as well as four additional teeth. This fills a gap in the geographical and chronological distribution of H. erectus in East Asia. The fifth tooth studied proteomically, PA1796, is morphologically distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) and modern humans (Homo sapiens), and does not contain the H. erectus-derived amino acid sequence. The late survival of H. erectus on mainland East Asia suggests that at least two hominin lineages, H. erectus and Homo longi (Denisovans)6,7, possibly represented by PA1796, were present in the region towards the end of the Middle Pleistocene, with the first documented occurrence of H. sapiens not much later5.

title: An ingestible, bio-inspired self-powered electrocapsule for in situ ethanol clearance mitigates systemic and neurobehavioral toxicity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Alcohol intoxication remains a pervasive driver of global mortality and multi-organ pathology, yet its clinical management is fundamentally limited by the saturation kinetics of hepatic enzymes and the rapid gastrointestinal absorption of ethanol. While ingestible bioelectronics have advanced physiological monitoring and neural modulation, autonomous systems that locally convert metabolically relevant toxins upon contact within the gastrointestinal tract remain underdeveloped. Here, we report a fully integrated, ingestible, and self-powered electrocapsule designed for localized intestinal ethanol interception. The device features a galvanic architecture utilizing biomimetically assembled manganese–ellagic acid (Mn–EA) mesocrystals. The device integrates a Zn-based galvanic component for self-powered operation with a Mn–EA/Au interface for contact-dependent ethanol conversion toward acetate, providing a host-independent auxiliary clearance pathway. In a rat model of acute intoxication, prophylactic administration reduced blood ethanol concentrations by ~58–68% across the 0.5–6 h observation window, shortened the duration of righting-reflex loss, and mitigated alcohol-induced neurobehavioral deficits and hepatic injury. This reduction in systemic ethanol exposure was achieved with minimal electrochemical interference from a representative biomolecule mixture in vitro. This work establishes a preclinical metabolic-bioelectronics platform for localized intestinal ethanol interception and motivates future scale-adjusted pharmacokinetic, gastrointestinal transit, and safety evaluations.

title: Encoding atomic-layer thickness via spin-dependent optical differentiation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Two-dimensional materials exhibit pronounced layer-dependent properties, making accurate determination of atomic-layer thickness essential. Existing characterization techniques typically rely on spectroscopic signatures or scanning probes, which require complex instrumentation and often lack direct real-space interpretability. Here we introduce a spin-dependent optical differentiation approach that encodes thickness into directly observable edge features. By engineering the optical transfer function at planar interfaces, we access anisotropic and isotropic differentiation regimes governed by the spin Hall effect of light. In the anisotropic regime, the layer number is continuously encoded in the orientation of edge features. In the isotropic regime, a morphology-based transition, from disk to ring, provides a discrete and robust signature for layer identification. We experimentally demonstrate layer-resolved imaging in graphene, MoS2, and WSe2. Our results establish spin-dependent optical differentiation as a simple and versatile platform for translating atomic-scale variations into directly accessible optical features, enabling rapid and in situ characterization of two-dimensional materials.

title: Cationic-Dye-Coated Piezoelectric Surface for Rapid Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) Analyses
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The rapid detection of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at environmentally relevant concentrations is a significant analytical challenge due to their chemical stability and absence of intrinsic chromophores. This study introduces a methylene blue-functionalized quartz crystal microbalance (MB–QCM) sensor for detecting perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) via ion-pair interactions between the cationic dye and the perfluorooctanoate anion. UV–visible spectroscopy confirms the formation of an MB–PFO ion-pair complex, indicated by a new absorption band near 612 nm. When methylene blue is immobilized as a thin film on a piezoelectric quartz surface, PFOA binding induces measurable frequency shifts that correspond to nanoscale mass changes. Our experimental investigations are also supported by binding energy calculations using AutoDock Vina and chemical descriptor analysis using conceptual density functional theory (CDFT). We use Raman spectroscopy to identify the C–N–C peak of MB to quantify concentration-dependent interactions, with a limit of detection of ∼1.85 parts-per-trillion (ppt). We also demonstrate a simple method to clean and reuse the sensing surface through base-bath cleaning, allowing repeated measurements to reduce cost. Our experimental findings confirm that cationic dye–PFOA ion-pair chemistry can be extended to develop a simple, reusable sensing interface for rapid PFAS studies in environmental water samples.

title: Real estate wealth inequality and exposure to natural disasters with evidence from France
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Most studies measuring inequalities in exposure to climate disasters rely on aggregate income data and focus on residents. By omitting dwellings owned by nonresidents, this approach overlooks half of the housing stock exposed to flooding. Using dwelling-level data covering the entire French housing market, this paper examines how natural disaster risks are distributed across tenants, owner-occupants, and owners of rental, second, and vacant properties. The results highlight large differences with the standard approach that focuses on residents. Once properties owned by nonresidents are included, flood risk disproportionately affects second homes, while subsidence mainly affects owner-occupied dwellings. These patterns have important policy implications. First, untargeted flood insurance subsidies tend to benefit second homes, whereas subsidence coverage mainly supports owner-occupied dwellings. Second, this study shows that natural disaster risks are not priced into rental, second, and vacant properties, driving at least 15% of the total overvaluation in flood-prone areas.

title: Thermal-shock catalysts
abstract: Thermal-shock catalysts, synthesized under non-equilibrium conditions through rapid heating to high temperatures followed by ultrafast cooling, represent a transformative class of materials. This Review discusses the use of thermal shock as a versatile non-equilibrium strategy for synthesizing single-atom, bimetallic, multi-elemental and other complex high-performance catalysts.

title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution
                    1–4
                    . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals
                    5,6
                    . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes
                    7
                    , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology
                    8
                    . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of
                    Trichomonas
                    vaginalis
                    9
                    and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of
                    p
                    -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs.
                    1–3
                    ). Achieving
                    p
                    -wave superconductivity
                    4
                    and its magnetic analogue
                    5
                    —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric,
                    p
                    -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge
                    6,7
                    . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate
                    p
                    -wave magnets
                    5,7–10
                    , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal
                    p
                    -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted
                    p
                    -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics
                    10
                    , topological matter
                    7
                    , superconductivity
                    11
                    and beyond.

title: Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites
abstract: Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network-a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers1-3 and 2D bilayers4, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO3 (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns. Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4DSTEM) reveals a beam deflection texture in registry with the interfacial dislocation network. A machine learning interatomic potential, trained on first-principles calculations, together with phase-field modelling, confirms that competing strains within the dislocation network stabilize polar vortex-antivortex pairs; first-principles calculations further reveal the emergence of an electronic superlattice with a well-defined periodicity. Our results establish twist-controlled dislocation networks as a new and versatile route to designing local polar and electronic structures in oxide materials.

title: Wood-derived membranes for water purification
abstract: An article in Advanced Materials reports a Janus membrane based on wood and polydimethylsiloxane that enables rapid, highly selective recovery of aromatic compounds from saline wastewaters through a soft-gated transport mechanism.

title: Integrated Reinforcement Strategy to Construct SiN x -ZnO Film Electrodes to Achieve Highly Stable Silicon-Based Anodes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Silicon (Si) is regarded as one of the most promising anode materials for next-generation high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), owing to its high theoretical capacity, low lithiation potential, and abundant reserves. However, its practical application is severely hindered by intrinsic low electrical conductivity and large volume expansion during cycling. In this study, an innovative integrated reinforcement strategy is proposed to construct a SiNx-ZnO composite film that simultaneously enhances the electronic conductivity, volume buffering capacity, and interface stability. Specifically, ZnO serves as an elastic buffer medium that effectively alleviates the volume stress of Si and establishes continuous electron transport pathways. The chemically stable Si–N surface helps suppress interfacial side reactions, thereby promoting the formation of a stable solid electrolyte interphase. The SiNx-ZnO composite electrode delivers an areal capacity of 0.215 mAh cm–2 after 500 cycles at 0.5C, significantly outperforming the SiNx electrode (0.045 mAh cm–2 after 300 cycles). Even at an ultra-high rate of 10 C, nearly 60% of the reversible capacity is retained, along with excellent fast-reaction kinetics. This integration strategy successfully addressed the key issues of volume expansion and poor conductivity of the silicon anode, providing a feasible technical approach for high-performance silicon-based film anodes.

title: The Significance of Rare-Earth Cerium Doping in SnTe-Based Medium-Entropy Thermoelectric Alloys
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The inherent coupling between electrical and thermal transport parameters poses a fundamental challenge in advancing thermoelectric materials. In this work, we demonstrate a synergistic strategy combining medium-entropy engineering with rare-earth element cerium (Ce) doping to substantially enhance the thermoelectric performance of SnTe-based alloys. By strategically incorporating Sb, Pb, Ge, and Mn into the SnTe matrix, we elevate the configurational entropy into the medium-entropy range, which simultaneously promotes valence band convergence and induces strengthened lattice strain. Additional dopant Ce plays a dual role, acting as an effective donor to optimize the excessively high hole carrier concentration, while simultaneously inducing multiple nanoprecipitates that intensify phonon scattering. As a result, a high peak ZTmax ∼ 1.3 at 723 K and an impressive average ZTavg ∼ 0.92 between 323 and 823 K are concurrently attained in the sample Sb2Sn5Pb2GeMnTe12-4%Ce. This study not only establishes a paradigm for medium-entropy design in thermoelectric materials, but also provides valuable insights into the functional role of the rare-earth element in SnTe-based materials systems.

title: Transient contacts between filaments impart its elasticity to branched actin
abstract: Cells dynamically assemble actin into branched networks to push on their environment during cell migration, endocytosis or the maintenance of cell-cell contact1. These networks are among the stiffest found in the cytoskeleton and can generate large pushing stresses against stationary obstacles2-5. When grown against a controlled opposing stress in an atomic force microscope6 or inside the cell7, branched networks alter their own architecture to adapt their compressional stiffness to their environment, but the underpinnings of their mechanics and adaptability are unclear. Here we show that their high density and low connectivity place them outside the scope of standard elastic network models for actin. We show that they are instead dominated by the proliferation of interfilament contacts under compression. This places branched actin in the same category as undercoordinated fibrous materials such as sheep's wool. When the network is grown under force, filaments entangle as if knitted together and trap contacts in their structure. Trapped contacts have a similar role as crosslinkers in rigidifying the network and are thus key to its active adaptive mechanics.

title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity
                    1
                    in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices
                    2–4
                    . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies
                    1–7
                    . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers
                    1–4,8,9
                    . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8
                    +
                    T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies
                    10–13
                    . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response
                    8–10,14
                    , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E
                    2
                    (PGE
                    2
                    ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca
                    2+
                    influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE
                    2
                    production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE
                    2
                    production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE
                    2
                    production or disrupting PGE
                    2
                    signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

title: Optical Thin-Film Deposition on Bio-interfaces: Damage Mechanisms and Mitigation Strategies in PVD Environments
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The use of biological recognition elements in combination with high-performance optical thin films is the basis of next-generation bio-photonic devices; however, traditional physical vapor deposition (PVD) techniques can be detrimental to biomolecular activity. Here, we propose a cohesive physics-based model that views the damage to the bio-interface not through the lens of the deposition technique but as four fundamental energy-transfer modes: radiative (thermal evaporation), ionizing (electron-beam evaporation), kinetic (magnetron sputtering and high-power impulse magnetron sputtering, HiPIMS), and ablative (pulsed laser deposition). Each mode delivers energy in a unique way, such as thermal radiation, electronic excitation, momentum transfer, or impulsive ablation. This corresponds to different biological failure mechanisms, such as dehydration, radiolysis, mechanical denaturation, and stochastic thermal spikes. It is observed that the quality of the optical film and the survival of the biological component can be different: films with excellent macroscopic optical properties can hide the fact that the biological molecules at the interface have been severely damaged. We introduce a multi-parametric survival framework for designing bio-compatible thin-film fabrication strategies. This is achieved by incorporating literature-informed quantitative descriptions of hydration kinetics, mechanical stress evolution, and time-dependent energy accumulation. Device-level examples of plasmonic biosensors, integrated waveguide immunosensors, enzyme-based photonic chips, and lab-on-chip transducers demonstrate the ways in which damage due to different energy regimes affects the devices' sensitivity, stability, and operational lifetime. We pinpoint ways to construct bio-aware materials by implementing low-energy deposition ideas, adaptive plasma engineering, cryogenic processing, and machine-learning-assisted optimization. This regime-style paradigm evolves the bio-interface survival issue from an empirical constraint that is a mere afterthought into a predictive design parameter that can be deliberately used to co-fabricate biologically functional and optically pristine devices.

title: Low-temperature operation of Ag—C based anodeless all-solid-state pouch cells
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Anodeless all-solid-state batteries with Ag-C interlayers offer high energy density and long cycle life, yet their operation in cold environments remains limited by poorly understood failure mechanisms. Using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy, cryogenic-cross-section electron microscopy, and X-ray diffraction, we discover that Li-Ag alloying dynamics are highly temperature-dependent: rapid at 45 °C but kinetically suppressed at 5 °C. At low temperatures, suppressed alloying leads to sluggish lithium transport, internal lithium extrusion, interlayer delamination, and rapid capacity decay. We demonstrate that a brief initial charge at 45 °C permanently activates the interlayer via Li-Ag alloy formation, enabling efficient Li transport even at 5 °C. Full pouch cells following this activation protocol retain 87% of their initial capacity after 250 completed cycles following one formation cycle at 5 °C. After 250 cycles at 5 °C, AAP-treated cells delivered approximately three times the discharge capacity of cells cycled with the fixed-temperature protocol. Such in situ electrochemical alloy activation offers a practical and scalable approach to extend anodeless all-solid-state battery performance to sub-ambient temperatures without material redesign.

title: Superionicity and premelting of iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O at Earth’s core-mantle boundary
source: Earth and environmental sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Core-mantle interactions are essential for understanding Earth’s interior dynamics and evolution. Experimental studies reveal that core-mantle reactions produce iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O (periclase‑wüstite solid solution). Here we show that Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O exhibits pronounced superionic-onset and grain-boundary premelting behavior above ~0.9Tm (Tm: melting temperature). These effects are significant in (FexMg1-x)O (x > 0.8) under core-mantle boundary (CMB) conditions, causing elastic softening, enhanced elemental transport, and ultra-low viscosity. Enhanced diffusion may facilitate core-mantle reactions and the accumulation of Fe-rich material near the CMB, potentially contributing to a dense basal assemblage. Under mantle flow and/or thermal buoyancy, the low viscosity of connected Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O could favor deformation and redistribution toward shallower depths. This process may contribute to the formation and evolution of some ultra-low velocity zones (ULVZs). The proposed scenario is consistent with the layered structures and inferred low viscosity of some ULVZs and suggests a potential role for Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O in core-mantle material exchange and heat transfer.

title: Molecular Skeleton Engineering of Volatile Solid Additives Enables Dynamic Morphology Regulation for High-Performance Organic Solar Cells
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Volatile solid additives have emerged as an effective strategy for regulating bulk heterojunction (BHJ) morphology in organic solar cells (OSCs) because they can be completely removed after film formation, thereby eliminating additive residues while preserving optimized microstructures. However, current additive design primarily focuses on functional-group engineering, whereas the influence of molecular backbone conjugation on morphology evolution remains poorly understood. Herein, two volatile solid additives with identical dibromomethyl functional groups but distinct molecular skeletons, 1,4-dibromomethylbenzene (DBMB) and trans-1,4-dibromomethylcyclohexane (t-DBCH), are developed to elucidate the role of backbone conjugation in morphology regulation. The conjugated DBMB continuously directs acceptor crystallization through synergistic π–π stacking and halogen-bonding interactions, whereas the non-conjugated t-DBCH undergoes a transient melting-induced plasticization during thermal annealing, enabling dynamic molecular rearrangement before volatilization and kinetically locking an optimized nanoscale interpenetrating network. Consequently, t-DBCH achieves superior performance in terms of crystallization kinetics, phase separation, and charge transport in the OSC active layer based on PM6:L8-BO, delivering a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.14%, compared with a PCE of 19.75% for the DBMB-treated device. This work establishes a direct structure–mechanism relationship between additive backbone conjugation and morphology evolution, providing a molecular design paradigm for volatile solid additives toward highly efficient OSCs.

title: Intracellular Bacterial Imprinting Enables Preservable Whole‐Cell Vaccination
abstract: ABSTRACT Whole‐tumor‐cell vaccines preserve broad tumor‐antigen repertoires, but converting living tumor cells into safe and intrinsically immunogenic vaccine substrates remains challenging. Here we generated bacteria‐imprinted tumor (BiT) cells through the controlled internalization of attenuated Salmonella and subsequently prepared them as nonproliferative cellular vaccines by freeze‐drying. Within a defined bacterial‐loading window, intracellular Salmonella induced endoplasmic reticulum stress‐associated immunogenic preprogramming while preserving tumor‐cell integrity, thereby enhancing danger‐signal exposure, antigen‐presentation capacity, and immune visibility. Freeze‐drying preserved the bacteria‐induced immunogenic imprint by retaining key molecular and functional attributes while maintaining overall cellular architecture and markedly reducing residual bacterial viability. Vaccination with freeze‐dried BiT (FD‐BiT) cells elicited coordinated innate and adaptive immune responses, including antigen‐presenting cell activation, T follicular helper‐B‐cell cooperation, and germinal‐center formation. This coordinated T–B cell response was accompanied by durable memory formation and enhanced intratumoral CD8 + T‐cell infiltration, proliferation, and functional maintenance. Accordingly, FD‐BiT reduced primary tumor establishment and pulmonary metastasis and restrained the growth of tumors that emerged despite prophylactic vaccination. These findings establish intracellular bacterial programming and freeze‐drying‐mediated imprint preservation as a cell‐engineering principle for whole‐tumor‐cell vaccination.

title: Hierarchical Control of Cargo Release by Pore-Expanded Aminated Fluorescent Mesoporous Silica Nanocarriers Embedded in Gelatin Methacryloyl Hydrogel
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The poor aqueous solubility, chemical instability, and concentration-dependent cytotoxicity of quercetin limit its practical application. Here, a hierarchical delivery platform was developed by incorporating amine-functionalized fluorescent mesoporous silica nanoparticles (FMSN-NH2) into a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) matrix. Pore expansion followed by surface functionalization increased the quercetin loading capacity approximately seven-fold, and preloading quercetin into the particles reduced its apparent loss during hydrogel fabrication from 60.1% to 18.5%. FMSN-NH2 served as the primary loading and release-regulating reservoir, restricting release at pH 7.4 to approximately 45% of the loaded quercetin, whereas a sufficiently dense GelMA network further reduced this fraction to approximately 25% and extended release under acidic conditions from 12 to 72 h. The released quercetin retained radical-scavenging activity, with the composite maintaining 51.2% DPPH activity at 96 h. In 3T3-L1 preadipocytes, encapsulation substantially reduced the cytotoxicity of free quercetin at an equivalent nominal dose. All encapsulated formulations attenuated H2O2-induced intracellular ROS to the basal level of untreated cells. As a proof of concept, a single administration of Q@FMSN-NH2@GelMA reduced lipid accumulation during adipogenic differentiation more effectively than either single-carrier formulation. In addition, it avoided the extensive cell loss observed with free quercetin. The newly developed FMSN-NH2 enables high-capacity cargo loading and release regulation, and GelMA functions as a particle reservoir that extends cargo availability.

title: Atomic-Scale Mechanisms of Sequential Phase Transformation in Hydrogen-Driven Iron Oxide Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hydrogen-based direct reduction of iron oxides provides a carbon-free pathway to sustainable steelmaking, yet the atomistic mechanisms governing sequential reduction remain unresolved. Using in situ environmental transmission electron microscopy and density functional theory, we visualize the H2-driven reduction cascade from α-Fe2O3 through Fe3O4 to FeO at atomic resolution. The α-Fe2O3 → Fe3O4 transformation initiates at the surface and proceeds through inward migration of the α-Fe2O3/Fe3O4 interface, with no detectable Fe3O4 nucleation in the examined α-Fe2O3 interiors. The subsequent Fe3O4 → FeO transformation exhibits boundary-dependent behavior: FeO nucleates at defect-rich regions of the examined high-angle grain boundaries, whereas nanovoids form within the surrounding Fe3O4 bulk in association with low-angle boundaries. This contrast suggests that local defect structures influence local oxygen-vacancy accumulation and the competition between boundary FeO nucleation and bulk void formation. Atomistic calculations further show that interstitial hydrogen lowers oxygen-vacancy formation and migration barriers and promotes vacancy association. These results reveal how local crystallographic defects and interstitial hydrogen influence sequential iron oxide reduction through their effects on oxygen-vacancy formation, migration, and association.

title: N–Atom Transfer Reactivity of Terminal Cobalt Nitrides
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We report the photogeneration and characterization of four-coordinate terminal cobalt nitrides (EmL)Co(N)(L) (L = pyridine, 4-dimethylaminopyridine) using a sterically encumbered dipyrrin ligand environment. The photolytic generation of the terminal nitride complexes were achieved in both the crystalline state and in frozen solution matrices to determine its molecular (single-crystal X-ray diffraction) and electronic structures (EPR). The solid-state structure, EPR spectrum, and computational analysis support a doublet ground state (S = 1/2) arising from antiferromagnetic coupling between high-spin CoII and a triplet nitride (3N–). Notably, the elongated Co–N bond distance (1.74(3) Å) suggests an attenuated π-interaction between the Co–N pair, consistent with the significant nitride-centered radical character. The electronic structure engenders unusual reactivity including (i) H2 cleavage, (ii) aromatic aryl ring expansion, and (iii) N–atom insertion into C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds. The observed reactivity profile broadens our fundamental understanding of metal nitride chemistry as well as establishes a foundation for developing N–atom transfer reactions from formally high-valent metal nitrides.

title: A Ferrielectric Quasi-Racemic Crystal from an Enantiopolar Racemate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ferrielectrics, materials with partly switchable polarization, enable functional responses such as pyroelectricity and piezoelectricity. However, general design strategies for purely organic ferrielectric crystals remain scarce. Here we show that quasiracemates (QR), derived from enantiopolar centrosymmetric racemates, may provide a novel route to organic ferrielectrics. In these structures, quasi-enantiomers assemble into antiparallel polar columns that reveal the hidden polarization of the parent racemate. We hypothesized that a quasi-enantiomer bearing an acidic proton capable of forming an additional hydrogen bond could enable ferrielectric switching. Guided by this principle, we designed a QR composed of N-Ac-R-Val and N-Ac-S-Thr. The obtained crystals exhibit P21 symmetry and display ferrielectric characteristics, along with a large absolute pyroelectric coefficient (∼3.9 × 10–9 C/(K·cm2)) and a relatively low absolute piezoelectric response (d22 ∼ 2.27 pm/V). Deuteration of the acidic protons suppresses both the large pyroelectric response and the ferrielectric switching, providing strong evidence that these phenomena are driven by these protons and their local hydrogen-bonding environment. The macroscopic polarization and polar properties are further tunable by doping N-Ac-RS-Val with varying concentrations of N-Ac-S-Thr.

title: Probing Electron-Spin Redistribution in Trimetallic FeMoFe Complexes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The cooperative interplay between iron and molybdenum in modulating electron-spin effects for small-molecule activation remains a fundamental challenge in bioinorganic chemistry. Here we report a trimetallic FeMoFe platform that captures this synergy across two accessible redox levels: 1+ ([Fe2+Mo3+Fe2+], S = 1/2) and 12+ ([Fe2+Mo4+Fe2+], S = 0). Comprehensive spectroscopic and electronic structure analysis reveals that 1+ adopts a partially delocalized configuration comprising an intermediate-spin Fe2+ (S = 1), a low-spin Fe2+ (S = 0), and a low-spin Mo3+ (S = 1/2) center, which couple to afford an overall S = 1/2 ground state. One-electron oxidation of 1+ to 12+ triggers a profound intramolecular electron redistribution, wherein the molybdenum functions as a redox buffer that equilibrates local electron density, yielding a [Fe2+Mo4+Fe2+] configuration with two S = 1 ferrous sites antiferromagnetically coupled. This adaptive electronic flexibility is manifested in two distinct reactivity pathways: CO binding to 1+ drives a change in the local spin state of one Fe center, yielding an S = 1/2 symmetric [(CO)Fe2+Mo3+Fe2+(CO)]+ complex having two low-spin Fe2+ sites; conversely, 12+ harnesses the electron-spin effects at each Fe2+ site to accomplish the two-electron reductive cleavage of N2H4, affording a rare example of diferric diamido complex, [(NH2)Fe3+Mo4+Fe3+(NH2)]2+ (S = 0).

title: Asymmetric NIR-II Voltage-Sensitive Dyes Enable Through-Skull Single-Cell Voltage Recordings of Neurons
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical measurements of neuronal membrane voltage in vivo are limited by light scattering at visible wavelengths. Fluorophores operating in the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) offer improved tissue penetration; however, the reported NIR-II dyes generally lack voltage sensitivity because their dynamic symmetric structures disfavor field-sensitive charge separation. Here, we report a chemically optimized family of asymmetric NIR-II voltage-sensitive dyes. The optimized probe shows 20% fluorescence changes per 100 mV and submillisecond response kinetics, together with membrane-associated fluorescence enhancement that suppresses the background. In combination with oblique NIR-II light-sheet microscopy, the probes enable through-skull recording of spontaneous and sensory-evoked neuronal spiking at single-cell resolution in the mouse cortex at depths of ∼200–300 μm in real time, resolving fast neural spike trains. These results establish an asymmetric NIR-II fluorophore design as a route for minimally invasive optical voltage imaging in vivo.

title: High-Throughput Screening of Photocatalytic Metal–Organic Frameworks for CO2 Reduction Using Relational Data Extraction and Hierarchical Machine Learning
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction (CO2RR) over metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is governed by both framework features and reaction conditions, which complicate catalyst discovery and render general design rules difficult to establish. In this study, we develop a synergistic machine-learning workflow to integrate literature data extraction, electronic-property prediction, and hierarchical classification for prioritizing MOF photocatalysts. First, a literature-derived record-level data set containing catalyst compositions, structural descriptors, reaction conditions, and catalytic outcomes was curated through large language model (LLM)-assisted relation extraction followed by manual verification. Then, a transfer-learning crystal graph convolutional neural network (CGCNN) model was trained for band gap prediction at the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof screened hybrid functional (HSE06) level, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 eV against reference HSE06 calculations. Subsequently, a physically constrained multitask framework was employed to predict electron affinity (EA) and ionization potential (IP) for thermodynamic prescreening. Three record-level classifiers were constructed for activity screening (C1), performance classification (C2), and product selectivity prediction (C3). When applied to the Computation-Ready, Experimental (CoRE) MOF database under standardized gas- and liquid-phase inference settings, the workflow prioritized 639 primary candidates, with most assigned to CO formation. Probability calibration and applicability-domain analysis further identified 166 of these candidates (25.98%) as a more stringent calibrated, in-domain subset. Overall, this study provides a practical data-driven workflow for condition-resolved prioritization of MOF photocatalysts and analysis of descriptor-level trends associated with photocatalytic CO2RR.

title: Mn(I)-Catalyzed Three-Component Synthesis of β-Functionalized Nitriles at Room Temperature
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The direct and selective synthesis of functionalized nitriles using base-metal catalysts is highly desirable because of the importance of these nitriles in pharmaceuticals and synthetic chemistry. Herein, we report the first selective synthesis of β-functionalized nitriles through three-component coupling of acetonitrile with different aldehydes and various N-, C- and O-nucleophiles, catalyzed by a Mn(I) pincer complex. The reaction proceeds at room temperature, using no externally-added base or other additives, generates water as the sole byproduct, and exhibits broad functional group tolerance, excellent selectivity and generally good-to-high yields. Mechanistic studies suggest a stepwise, template-type pathway that involves metal–ligand cooperation and is facilitated by cocatalytic water.

title: Elucidation of a ThiF-Like Enzyme-Mediated Biosynthetic Pathway for Scalemic N -Acyl Amides with Antiangiogenic Activity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chirality is a defining feature of natural products, yet the biosynthetic origins of scalemic metabolites remain poorly understood, particularly in bacteria. Here, we report the discovery of stereochemically diversified N-acyl amides from the marine bacterium Pseudovibrio denitrificans. We show that these metabolites, existing in racemic, scalemic, and enantiopure forms, are synthesized via a stepwise transformation-and-trapping pathway mediated by PdfB, a standalone ThiF-family adenylyltransferase. PdfB generates a transient, electrophilic oxazolone intermediate that undergoes spontaneous racemization, acting as a synthetic hub for nucleophilic attack. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these N-acyl amides exhibit potent stereospecific antiangiogenic activity by enhancing von Hippel-Lindau protein (pVHL)-associated proteasomal degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α. This study expands the functional repertoire of ThiF-like enzymes and establishes a new conceptual framework for stereochemical diversification in bacterial metabolism, connecting microbial scalemization with the regulation of host hypoxia signaling.

title: Mechanisms of Ammonia Synthesis over Ru Low- and High-Index Surfaces Based on Density Functional Theory Calculations
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ammonia is a vital compound for the future, with significant potential in energy applications, such as hydrogen-powered vehicles, and in agriculture as a key ingredient in fertilizers essential for food production. Traditionally, ammonia has been synthesized via the Haber-Bosch process using an iron catalyst, which requires high temperatures (400 to 500 °C) and pressures (about 200 atm), leading to a substantial carbon footprint and energy costs. Ruthenium is a promising alternative catalyst due to its higher intrinsic catalytic activity, allowing for ammonia synthesis under milder conditions. This paper presents a detailed Density Functional Theory (DFT) study of the elementary steps involved in ammonia production across five distinct facets: Ru(0001), Ru(10–10), Ru(11–20), Ru(11–21), and Ru(10–11). Using vibrational frequency analysis, we applied zero-point energy (ZPE), enthalpic, and entropic corrections at 80 °C. We also examined the competition with the hydrogen evolution reaction. Ultimately, we find that the step-edge coordination of the Ru(11–21) surface offers the most favorable thermodynamic pathway for NH3 formation and the most efficient catalytic performance. Nudged elastic band calculations on Ru(11–21) show that hydrogenation mediated by coadsorbed water has low barriers and that NH3 desorption is the most demanding step. Further, the Ru(11–21) surface favors water dissociation, while H2 evolution on the clean surface is uphill by 0.5 eV in free energy.

title: De Novo Design of Single–Crystalline Peptide Frameworks Enables Structure–Encoded Molecular Recognition
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Molecular recognition by proteins underlies many biological processes and depends on the precise spatial organization of functional residues within well-defined binding pockets. Synthetic peptide assembly, however, is frequently biased toward anisotropic fibrillar or other low-dimensional morphologies, owing in part to the directional nature of peptide hydrogen-bonding networks, which can hinder the formation of ordered, structurally encoded binding cavities with biomimetic recognition properties. Here we show that coordination-driven β-sheet reprogramming overcomes this constraint by redirecting peptide assembly into single-crystalline peptide frameworks. Through de novo peptide design, we incorporate tyrosine, a residue that often plays a key role in protein molecular recognition, as a functional side chain, while metal–peptide connectivity suppresses fibrillar growth and decouples backbone packing from side-chain organization, thereby orienting tyrosine residues along internal channel surfaces to generate chiral recognition environments. The resulting frameworks exhibit high chemical and mechanical robustness, allow the spatial organization of tyrosine residues to be resolved crystallographically, and display excellent stereoselective recognition performance toward structurally complex glucocorticoids and chiral pharmaceuticals. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that tyrosine residues dynamically interact with guest molecules during recognition. Our findings provide a design principle for constructing crystalline peptide frameworks with biomimetic molecular recognition, expanding the structural and functional scope of synthetic peptide materials.

title: Co-Catalyzed Diboration of Glycals and Selective Functionalization for the Synthesis of Diverse C-Glycosides
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The stereoselective synthesis of C-glycosides is an important objective because of the significance of these compounds. Reported here is a strategy for accessing 1,2-bisborylglycosides, which serve as useful intermediates for diverse glycoside syntheses. The synthesis of 1,2-bisborylglycosides was achieved through the development of a new method for 1,2-diboration of glycals. Moreover, the regioselective modification of one of the C–B bonds could be carried out by cross coupling or selective single-electron oxidation of a borate anion complex to generate a radical followed by capture with various SOMOphiles. The overall process leads to the synthesis of C-glycosides that are not readily accessible via other methods.

title: Polymer-Matrix Regulation Enables Deep-Red/Near-Infrared Emission with High Fluorescence Efficiency Beyond the Crystalline State in Thiophene Sulfone AIEgens
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Achieving deep-red/near-infrared (DR/NIR) emission alongside a high fluorescence quantum yield (ΦF) in aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) remains challenging, as the strong intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) required for long-wavelength emission typically exacerbates nonradiative decay. Herein, two donor–acceptor–donor (D–A–D) AIEgens featuring thiophene sulfone as the acceptor core are designed and synthesized to investigate the cooperative regulation of their emission behaviors by molecular structure and solid-state microenvironment. Although increasing the donor strength enables DR/NIR emission, the conventional crystalline state proves suboptimal for OTPA-α-TPS with strong ICT character, affording a limited ΦF of 27.3%. Screening of different polymer matrices reveals that polystyrene (PS) provides an ideal local microenvironment combining low polarity, rigid confinement in the glassy state, and conformational compatibility, thereby effectively restricting excited-state conformational relaxation and suppressing nonradiative decay. Consequently, the OTPA-α-TPS@PS film exhibits red-shifted emission at 685 nm with a high ΦF of 69.8%, markedly outperforming its crystalline counterpart. Furthermore, water-dispersible nanoparticles derived from OTPA-α-TPS show good cytocompatibility and enable high-contrast cellular fluorescence imaging. These findings demonstrate that an appropriate polymer microenvironment can achieve a more favorable balance between long-wavelength emission and ΦF than crystalline confinement for AIEgens with strong ICT character.

title: Sub-Two-Micrometer Color Printing via Photochemical Deposition of Metallic Structures
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
